title: Competitive & OA Toolbox
relevance: OA hard problems are often a standard CP technique in disguise; this toolbox turns unknown patterns into known modular, number-theory, and search templates.

phases.goal: Establish the core modular, number-theory, and pattern-recognition primitives that OA hard problems reuse.

must_hit.point: Addition, subtraction, and multiplication distribute over modulo, but division does not.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states that +/−/× can be reduced mod m safely, while division needs a modular inverse instead of direct /.

must_hit.point: When m is prime, modular inverse of b is b^{m-2} mod m by Fermat's Little Theorem, computed via binary exponentiation in O(log m).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions Fermat for prime moduli and inverse as pow(b, m-2), not trial search.

must_hit.point: Sieve of Eratosthenes finds all primes up to n in O(n log log n); trial division factorizes one x in O(√x).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Quotes both sieve and single-number trial-division complexities correctly.

must_hit.point: LCM is a·b / gcd(a,b); C++17 provides std::gcd and std::lcm in <numeric>.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the LCM identity and where the standard helpers live.

probes: When a problem asks for answers modulo a prime, how do you handle division, and why can't you just divide then mod?
What does the Sieve of Eratosthenes buy you versus trial-dividing one number?

hints.1: Think about which arithmetic ops survive modulo reduction unchanged.
hints.2: For prime m, connect Fermat’s Little Theorem to inverse and binary exponentiation.
hints.3: Division → multiply by b^{m-2}; sieve is O(n log log n) for all primes; one x is O(√x) trial division.

phases.goal: Check that the candidate can execute the main toolbox algorithms correctly end-to-end.

must_hit.point: Binary exponentiation computes x^n in O(log n) via x^n = (x^{n/2})^2 for even n and x · x^{n-1} for odd n.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes the even/odd recurrence and log-time loop, not naive repeated multiply.

must_hit.point: Precompute factorials and inverse factorials for O(1) nCr mod m after O(N) setup.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains fact/invFact arrays and nCr as fact[n]*invFact[r]*invFact[n-r].

must_hit.point: SPF sieve precomputes in O(n log log n) so any x ≤ n factorizes in O(log x) by repeatedly dividing by spf[x].
must_hit.evidence_hint: Distinguishes SPF precompute from per-query loop that peels smallest prime factors.

must_hit.point: Extended Euclidean finds x,y with a·x + b·y = gcd(a,b), used for Diophantine equations, linear congruences, and inverses when m is not prime.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States Bezout coefficients and non-prime inverse use case.

must_hit.point: Coordinate compression maps large values to dense ranks in [0,k) with k ≤ N by sorting, unique, and lower_bound ranks.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks sort → dedupe → rank replace; mentions BIT/segtree indexing motivation.

must_hit.point: Matrix exponentiation raises a k×k transition matrix in O(k^3 log n) to get the n-th term of a linear recurrence in O(log n) for fixed small k.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Ties Fibonacci-style transition matrix to binary matrix powering complexity.

probes: Walk through computing modular nCr after preprocessing, and how SPF factorization of one x works.
How do you compute the n-th Fibonacci with matrix exponentiation, and what is the cost in terms of matrix size k?

hints.1: Separate precomputation from the per-query formula.
hints.2: For SPF: while x≠1, push spf[x] and x/=spf[x]; for matrices, identity then square-and-multiply.
hints.3: nCr = fact[n]*invFact[r]*invFact[n-r]; matrix pow is O(k^3 log n); Fib transition [[1,1],[1,0]].

phases.goal: Compare when to pick SPF vs trial division, MITM vs full brute force, and related overflow-safe formulations.

must_hit.point: Factorize many numbers ≤ n with SPF (O(log x) each after sieve) rather than O(√x) trial division per number.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Chooses SPF for batch factorization and trial division for a one-off x.

must_hit.point: Meet in the Middle cuts O(2^n) backtracking to O(2^{n/2} log(2^{n/2})) by splitting into halves, enumerating subset sums, and combining with sort/binary search.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States split, enumerate both halves, then O(K log K)-style combine with K=2^{n/2}.

must_hit.point: In the band 20 ≤ N ≤ 40, full 2^40 is hopeless while each 2^20 half is feasible; below 20 plain brute force is fine.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses the 20–40 recognition window and contrasts 2^20 vs 2^40 scale.

must_hit.point: Compute LCM as (a/gcd(a,b))*b, not (a*b)/gcd, to avoid intermediate overflow.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the overflow-safe LCM order explicitly.

probes: When would you use SPF sieve versus trial division, and when does Meet in the Middle beat plain subset enumeration?
Why is LCM written as (a/gcd)*b instead of (a*b)/gcd?

hints.1: Ask whether you factor once or many times, and whether N sits in a special range.
hints.2: MITM: split N/2, enumerate both, stitch with sort/search; LCM: divide before multiply.
hints.3: Many x≤n → SPF O(log x); 20≤N≤40 subset problems → MITM; LCM=(a/gcd)*b.

phases.goal: Apply recognition checklists: MITM constraints, huge-N linear recurrences, and the stuck-on-OA playbook.

must_hit.point: Recognize Meet in the Middle when N is about 30–40, the task is subset/choice, DP is blocked (e.g. |nums[i]| ≤ 10^9 or negatives/multi-constraints), and halves combine in O(K log K) or O(K).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Hits the four-check recognition: golden N range, subset/choice, DP impossible, efficient combine.

must_hit.point: If you need the N-th term of a linear recurrence with N up to 10^18, matrix exponentiation is the intended approach.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Flags huge N on a linear recurrence as matrix-pow, not iterative DP.

must_hit.point: Coordinate compression is mandatory when values are up to 10^9 but N is small (e.g. 10^5) and you need them as BIT/segtree indices.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links huge value domain + small N + index structure to compression.

must_hit.point: Stuck checklist: monotonic search space → binary search on answer; graph in disguise → BFS/Dijkstra; DP min/max/ways; math/counting identity; range queries → segment tree, dynamic median → two heaps.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists several of the five angles from the interview checklist without inventing extras.

probes: An array problem has N around 40 and values up to 10^9 asking for closest subset sum to a goal—what do you try and why not DP?
Walk the 'I'm stuck' checklist you would run on an OA problem that looks impossible.

hints.1: Look at N and value magnitude before building a DP table.
hints.2: For MITM: split, enumerate subset sums, binary-search the other half; for huge Fib-like N use matrix pow.
hints.3: N~40 + huge values → MITM (e.g. Closest Subsequence Sum); N up to 10^18 linear recurrence → matrix exp; then run the five stuck angles.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: One-off factorization of x uses O(√x) trial division; many factorizations of values ≤ n use SPF precomputation in O(n log log n) then O(log x) per query.

tradeoffs.topic: Full 2^n brute force vs Meet in the Middle
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Below ~20, enumerate subsets directly; in 20≤N≤40 split into halves so each side is ~2^{n/2}, then combine with sort/binary search in O(2^{n/2} log(2^{n/2})) instead of impossible 2^n.
For prime m, inverse via binpow(b, m-2); when m is not prime, use Extended Euclidean for Bezout coefficients / modular inverse.
Prefer (a/gcd(a,b))*b over (a*b)/gcd(a,b) so the intermediate product does not overflow.
Avoid rand() (outdated, small period, predictable); use std::mt19937 (Mersenne Twister) for randomization.

gotchas.trap: Multiplying two 32-bit ints then taking modulo, assuming the mod prevents overflow.
gotchas.correction: Overflow happens before modulo; cast to long long (or multiply in 64-bit) before the product.
Use (a/gcd(a,b))*b to avoid overflow on the intermediate a*b.

gotchas.trap: Trying DP on a subset-sum style problem with N~30–40 and values up to 10^9.
gotchas.correction: DP indexed by sum blows memory; use Meet in the Middle: split halves, enumerate both, combine with sort/search.
Use mt19937 seeded from a high-resolution clock (or similar), not rand().

gotchas.trap: Forgetting that subtraction mod m can go negative.
gotchas.correction: Normalize with forms like (a - b%MOD + MOD) % MOD so results stay non-negative.

gotchas.trap: Heavy I/O with tied streams and endl causing TLE.
gotchas.correction: Untie cin from cout and avoid endl (fast I/O) as in the OA survival guidance.
